plan: Two passages weighted toward Key Ideas and Details (15 of 20): CLD-P-ACT-R-000076, original literary narrative (two sisters share their late grandmother's annotated recipe box; third-person narration); CLD-P-ACT-R-000077, natural science on sunflower solar tracking (Harmer lab, UC Davis, 2016: differential stem growth, internal clock, growth benefit, east-facing mature heads warming faster and drawing about five times as many pollinators, heater test). Topics checked against both workstreams. Plus R073-20 (revision 2) on banked passage CLD-P-ACT-R-000075. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Righter
passages.text:
The recipe box had sat on top of their grandmother's refrigerator for as long as either sister could remember: a dented tin box, painted with faded strawberries, its lid held shut by a rubber band. After the funeral, it was the only thing Lena and Ruth both asked for. Their mother, tired of mediating, told them to sort it out between themselves.

So on a Sunday in March they sat across from each other at Lena's kitchen table, the box between them. Lena, the older by six years, had already proposed a system. They would photograph every card, divide the originals by category, and each keep a complete set of copies. Ruth, who had driven three hours to get there, said that sounded fine, in the voice she used when nothing sounded fine.

The cards themselves were not what either of them had expected. Their grandmother had been a famously confident cook, but the margins of nearly every card were crowded with notes in her slanting hand. "Too salty—half next time." "Tried with honey. No." "Better with the old oven." On the card for the apple cake that had appeared at every family birthday, there were eleven dated entries, the earliest from 1962 and the last from two years ago, each changing something small.

"She never got it right," Ruth said, sounding almost delighted.

"She got it right every time," Lena said. "She just kept trying to get it righter." She heard herself and laughed, and after a moment Ruth laughed too, the first time they had laughed together since the hospital.

They abandoned Lena's system before lunch. Instead, they read the cards aloud to each other, arguing over which notes were jokes and which were serious, and by evening they had decided that neither of them would take the box. It would go back and forth between their two houses, a season at a time, and whoever had it would bake one recipe from it and add a note of her own in the margin.

passages.title: Facing the Sun
passages.text:
Anyone who has watched a field of young sunflowers over the course of a day may have noticed something remarkable: the plants turn. In the morning their tops face east, toward the rising sun; by evening they have swung around to face west. Overnight, they turn back toward the east, ready for sunrise.

In 2016, plant biologist Stacey Harmer and her colleagues at the University of California, Davis, published a study of how and why this happens. They found that the turning is produced by uneven growth. During the day, cells on the east side of the stem grow faster than those on the west side, bending the top of the plant westward; at night, the west side grows faster, bending it back. When the researchers moved plants indoors under a fixed overhead light, the plants continued to sway on a roughly daily schedule for several days, suggesting that an internal clock helps control the movement.

The tracking appears to benefit the young plants. When the researchers staked some plants so that they could not turn, or rotated their pots each day so that they faced away from the sun, those plants grew less than plants that tracked normally.

As sunflowers mature and their flower heads open, however, the turning slows and then stops, and most of the flowers end up facing east. The researchers suspected that this orientation was not an accident. In field tests, east-facing flower heads warmed up more quickly in the morning sun than west-facing ones, and they received about five times as many visits from bees and other pollinators. When the researchers used a heater to warm west-facing heads in the morning, those flowers attracted more pollinators too.

The sunflower's daily turn, then, is not one behavior but two: a youthful habit that helps the plant grow, followed by a fixed position that helps it reproduce.

passages.title: Riverbank Beginnings
passages.text:
Kabuki, one of the great theatrical traditions of Japan, began not on a stage but on a riverbank. Around 1603, a performer named Izumo no Okuni began presenting dances and comic sketches on the dry bed of the Kamo River in Kyoto. Her troupe, made up largely of women, drew large crowds with flamboyant costumes and scenes from everyday life, and other troupes soon imitated her.

The new entertainment was popular, but the authorities of the Tokugawa shogunate viewed it with suspicion. In 1629, they banned women from performing on the kabuki stage, concerned about the rowdy crowds and the social mixing the performances encouraged. Troupes of young men took their place, but these too were banned in 1652. From then on, kabuki was performed by adult men alone.

It would be easy to see these bans only as a loss, and in one sense they were: the women who had created kabuki were shut out of it for centuries. Yet the restrictions also produced one of kabuki's most admired arts. Actors known as onnagata devoted their careers to playing women's roles, and because they could not rely on simply being women, they built their portrayals out of carefully studied gestures, postures, and ways of speaking. Their art was not an imitation of how women actually behaved so much as a stylized idea of femininity, refined over generations and passed from teacher to student.

Some of the most celebrated actors in kabuki's history were onnagata, and audiences came to value their performances precisely because of their artifice. A great onnagata was admired not for persuading viewers that they were watching a woman but for the skill with which every movement had been shaped.

The story of kabuki's beginnings is thus a reminder that artistic traditions are shaped by forces outside art as well as within it. A government decree intended to control public behavior helped create one of the theater's most distinctive forms, one that has outlasted the government that imposed it.

candidates.stem: Which of the following best describes what happens in the passage?

choices.A: Two sisters compete to prove which of them is the better cook by baking the same recipes.
choices.B: Two sisters who disagree over a keepsake find a way to share it that brings them closer.
choices.C: A grandmother teaches her granddaughters to cook during a series of Sunday visits.
choices.D: Two sisters discover that their grandmother's famous recipes were copied from a cookbook.

candidates.evidence: It would go back and forth between their two houses
candidates.explanation: The sisters begin divided over the recipe box and end by agreeing to share it, laughing together for the first time since the hospital.

A.rationale: They do not compete over cooking; they agree to share the box.

C.rationale: The grandmother has died; the sisters read her cards.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests the recipes were copied.

hints: How are the sisters getting along at the start and at the end?

strategy.explanation: Compare the opening and closing paragraphs.

candidates.remember: A narrative's main idea usually involves a change.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, Lena's original plan was for the sisters to:

choices.A: take turns keeping the recipe box for a season at a time.
choices.B: give the box back to their mother to keep in her kitchen.
choices.C: photograph the cards, divide the originals, and each keep copies.
choices.D: choose one recipe each and leave the rest of the cards in the box.

candidates.evidence: They would photograph every card, divide the originals by category
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes Lena's system: photograph every card, divide the originals, and each keep a set of copies.

A.rationale: This is the plan they adopt later, not Lena's original proposal.

B.rationale: Their mother told them to sort it out themselves.

D.rationale: Lena's plan involved photographing every card.

hints: What does paragraph 2 say Lena proposed?

strategy.explanation: Distinguish the first plan from the final one.

candidates.remember: Watch for answers that describe a different moment in the story.

candidates.stem: The description of Ruth's voice in paragraph 2 ("the voice she used when nothing sounded fine") most strongly suggests that Ruth:

choices.A: was unhappy with Lena's plan but did not say so directly.
choices.B: was too tired from her drive to listen to Lena's plan.
choices.C: thought Lena's plan was a fair and sensible solution.
choices.D: planned to take the recipe box home without telling Lena.

candidates.evidence: in the voice she used when nothing sounded fine
candidates.explanation: Ruth says the plan sounds fine, but in a tone she uses when nothing is fine, so she disapproves without saying so.

B.rationale: Her voice signals displeasure, not inattention.

C.rationale: The phrase suggests the opposite of approval.

hints: What does the tone reveal that the words do not?

strategy.explanation: Contrast what Ruth says with how she says it.

candidates.remember: A character's tone can contradict her words.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the notes in the margins of the recipe cards included all of the following EXCEPT:

choices.A: a reminder to use only half as much of an ingredient next time.
choices.B: a record of a failed experiment with honey.
choices.C: a comment comparing results with an older oven.
choices.D: instructions for how the grandmother wanted the box divided.

candidates.evidence: "Too salty—half next time."
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 quotes notes about salt, honey, and an old oven, but none about dividing the box.

A.rationale: "Too salty—half next time" is one of the notes.

B.rationale: "Tried with honey. No." is one of the notes.

C.rationale: "Better with the old oven" is one of the notes.

hints: Which notes does paragraph 3 quote?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the quoted notes.

candidates.remember: For EXCEPT questions, eliminate choices the passage supports.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the card for the apple cake contained:

choices.A: eleven dated entries spanning roughly six decades.
choices.B: a single note saying the recipe should never be changed.
choices.C: instructions written by the sisters' mother.
choices.D: a list of the birthdays when the cake had been served.

candidates.evidence: there were eleven dated entries, the earliest from 1962
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the card had eleven dated entries, from 1962 to two years before, each changing something small.

B.rationale: The card has many entries, each changing something.

C.rationale: The notes are in the grandmother's hand.

D.rationale: The entries record changes, not birthdays.

hints: What does paragraph 3 say about the apple cake card?
candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the text.

candidates.stem: When Lena says that her grandmother "just kept trying to get it righter" (paragraph 5), she most nearly means that her grandmother:

choices.A: never managed to make a recipe that her family enjoyed.
choices.B: was always willing to improve recipes that were already good.
choices.C: made careless mistakes that she had to correct later.
choices.D: wanted her granddaughters to finish her unfinished recipes.

candidates.evidence: She got it right every time
candidates.explanation: Lena insists the recipes were already right and that her grandmother kept refining them anyway.

A.rationale: Lena says she "got it right every time."

C.rationale: Lena presents the changes as refinements, not corrections of mistakes.

hints: What does Lena say just before "righter"?

strategy.explanation: Read the statement with the sentence before it.

candidates.remember: Interpret a playful word using its context.

author_checklist.hardness: playful coinage interpreted against a contrasting claim

candidates.stem: Ruth's reaction to the notes ("She never got it right," said "almost delighted") suggests that Ruth:

choices.A: was disappointed to learn that the beloved family recipes were flawed.
choices.B: wanted to prove to Lena that she was the better cook of the two sisters.
choices.C: was pleased to see that their confident grandmother had also struggled.
choices.D: believed the recipe cards had been written by someone else.

candidates.evidence: Their grandmother had been a famously confident cook
candidates.explanation: Finding many corrections from a "famously confident" cook delights Ruth, suggesting pleasure at seeing her grandmother's ordinary struggles.

B.rationale: The remark concerns their grandmother, not the sisters' cooking.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests she doubted the handwriting.

hints: What was surprising about the notes, given the grandmother's reputation?
candidates.remember: Infer a character's feeling from her reaction and its context.

author_checklist.hardness: reaction must be linked to an earlier detail

candidates.stem: Which of the following events occurs last in the passage?

choices.A: Lena proposes photographing every card.
choices.B: The sisters laugh together for the first time since the hospital.
choices.C: Ruth remarks that their grandmother never got the recipe right.
choices.D: The sisters decide that the box will move between their houses.

candidates.evidence: by evening they had decided that neither of them would take the box
candidates.explanation: The decision to pass the box back and forth comes in the final paragraph, by evening.

B.rationale: This happens in paragraph 5, before their decision.

hints: Which paragraph contains each event?
candidates.remember: Track the order of events by paragraph.

candidates.stem: The sisters' final arrangement, in which each will add a note to the margins, suggests that they:

choices.A: want to continue their grandmother's habit of revising and recording.
choices.B: plan to replace their grandmother's notes with their own.
choices.C: intend to publish their grandmother's recipes together as a cookbook.
choices.D: no longer value the recipe cards as much as they did before that day.

candidates.evidence: add a note of her own in the margin
candidates.explanation: Adding notes as their grandmother did continues her practice of testing and recording changes.

B.rationale: They will add notes, not replace hers.

D.rationale: The arrangement shows they value the cards more.

hints: Whose habit does adding margin notes imitate?
candidates.remember: Endings often echo details from earlier in a story.

author_checklist.hardness: ending must be linked back to paragraph 3

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 1, the word "mediating" most nearly means:

choices.A: preparing large meals for family gatherings.
choices.B: settling disagreements between other people.
choices.C: thinking quietly and deeply about the past.
choices.D: sorting objects into categories.

candidates.evidence: told them to sort it out between themselves
candidates.explanation: The mother is tired of handling the sisters' dispute, so "mediating" means settling disagreements between them.

A.rationale: The context is the sisters' disagreement, not cooking.

D.rationale: Sorting is what the sisters are told to do, not what the mother is tired of.

hints: What is the mother tired of doing?

strategy.explanation: Substitute each choice into the sentence.

candidates.remember: Watch for words that look like other words.

candidates.stem: The main idea of the passage is that sunflowers:

choices.A: turn with the sun while young and later face east, and both habits help them.
choices.B: always face east because morning sunlight is the most useful to plants.
choices.C: turn toward the sun only because they are following its light at every moment.
choices.D: grow best when gardeners rotate their pots so that they face away from the sun.

candidates.evidence: a youthful habit that helps the plant grow, followed by a fixed position that helps it reproduce
candidates.explanation: The passage explains the young plants' daily turning, its benefit for growth, and the mature flowers' east-facing position, which helps attract pollinators.

B.rationale: Young sunflowers turn east and west each day.

C.rationale: The passage suggests an internal clock also controls the movement.

D.rationale: Plants rotated away from the sun grew less.

hints: What two behaviors does the last paragraph name?

strategy.explanation: Read the conclusion, then check it against each paragraph.

candidates.remember: A main-idea answer must include the passage's conclusion.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, during the day the top of a young sunflower bends westward because:

choices.A: cells on the west side of its stem shrink in the afternoon heat.
choices.B: cells on the east side of its stem grow faster than those on the west side.
choices.C: the stem becomes weaker as the day gets warmer.
choices.D: the leaves become heavier on the west side as they slowly fill with water.

candidates.evidence: During the day, cells on the east side of the stem grow faster
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 says faster growth on the east side during the day bends the plant westward.

A.rationale: The passage describes faster growth on one side, not shrinking.

hints: What does paragraph 2 say happens during the day?
candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the text.

candidates.stem: The results of moving plants indoors under a fixed overhead light suggest that:

choices.A: sunflowers stop growing altogether whenever they are kept indoors for long.
choices.B: artificial light causes sunflowers to turn much faster than natural sunlight does.
choices.C: the sunflowers' movement is not driven solely by the changing position of the sun.
choices.D: sunflowers need a fixed light source in order to survive.

candidates.evidence: suggesting that an internal clock helps control the movement
candidates.explanation: Because the plants kept swaying on a daily schedule without a moving sun, something internal must help drive the movement.

A.rationale: The passage says the plants kept swaying, not that they stopped growing.

B.rationale: Speed of turning under different lights is not compared.

hints: What was missing indoors that is present outdoors?
candidates.remember: An experiment shows what still happens when a factor is removed.

author_checklist.hardness: must reason from a controlled condition

candidates.stem: According to paragraph 3, plants that were prevented from tracking the sun:

choices.A: produced noticeably more flowers than other plants.
choices.B: turned east earlier in the season.
choices.C: attracted fewer bees to their leaves.
choices.D: grew less than plants that tracked normally.

candidates.evidence: those plants grew less than plants that tracked normally
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 says staked or rotated plants grew less.

B.rationale: Paragraph 3 does not discuss turning east.

C.rationale: Pollinators are discussed in paragraph 4, for flower heads.

hints: What does the end of paragraph 3 say?
candidates.remember: Do not mix details from different paragraphs.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, as sunflowers mature, their turning:

choices.A: slows and then stops, with most flowers facing east.
choices.B: speeds up to follow the sun more closely.
choices.C: reverses so that the flowers face west each morning.
choices.D: continues unchanged until the flowers wilt.

candidates.evidence: the turning slows and then stops, and most of the flowers end up facing east
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the turning slows and stops, and most flowers end up facing east.

C.rationale: Most flowers end up facing east.

hints: What does paragraph 4 say happens as sunflowers mature?
candidates.remember: Track how a process changes over time.

candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 4, east-facing flower heads differed from west-facing ones in that east-facing heads:

choices.A: produced more seeds but attracted fewer pollinators.
choices.B: stayed cooler throughout the day and lasted longer.
choices.C: warmed up faster in the morning and drew more pollinators.
choices.D: turned to follow the sun for a much longer period of time.

candidates.evidence: east-facing flower heads warmed up more quickly in the morning sun
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 says east-facing heads warmed faster in the morning and received about five times as many pollinator visits.

A.rationale: East-facing heads attracted more pollinators; seed counts are not given.

hints: What two differences does paragraph 4 report?
candidates.remember: Keep track of which detail belongs to which group.

candidates.stem: The heater experiment described in paragraph 4 was most likely designed to test whether:

choices.A: sunflowers can survive cold nights in the field.
choices.B: morning warmth itself is what attracts pollinators to east-facing flowers.
choices.C: west-facing flowers produce less nectar in the morning than east-facing ones.
choices.D: pollinators prefer flowers that are farther from the ground.

candidates.evidence: When the researchers used a heater to warm west-facing heads in the morning
candidates.explanation: Warming west-facing heads separates warmth from direction; if they then draw more pollinators, warmth is the attracting factor.

A.rationale: Surviving cold nights is not the question the experiment addresses.

hints: What did the heater change, and what did it leave the same?

strategy.explanation: Identify the variable the experiment isolated.

candidates.remember: Experiments isolate one factor to test its effect.

candidates.stem: The main function of the last paragraph is to:

choices.A: summarize the passage by distinguishing two stages of the plant's behavior.
choices.B: introduce a new experiment whose results challenge the earlier findings.
choices.C: argue that young sunflowers do not actually turn toward the sun.
choices.D: describe the people who were the first to notice that sunflowers turn.

candidates.evidence: is not one behavior but two
candidates.explanation: The final paragraph sums up the passage: the young plant's turning helps growth, and the mature flower's fixed position helps reproduction.

C.rationale: The paragraph confirms that they do.

D.rationale: The paragraph does not discuss the first observers.

hints: What does "not one behavior but two" summarize?

strategy.explanation: Relate the last paragraph to the rest of the passage.

candidates.remember: Concluding paragraphs often summarize and generalize.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word "accident" most nearly means:

choices.A: harmful mishap.
choices.B: sudden collision.
choices.C: careless error.
choices.D: chance result.

candidates.evidence: this orientation was not an accident
candidates.explanation: The researchers suspected the east-facing orientation had a purpose rather than being a chance result.

C.rationale: No one made an error; the question is whether the orientation was purposeful.

hints: What did the researchers suspect about the orientation?

strategy.explanation: Substitute each choice into the sentence.

candidates.remember: Choose the meaning that fits the context.

choices.A: a university in the eastern United States.
choices.B: a government agriculture laboratory.
choices.C: the University of California, Davis.
choices.D: a botanical garden in Europe.

hints: Where does paragraph 2 say the researchers worked?

candidates.stem: In the last paragraph, the author suggests that kabuki's history shows that artistic traditions can be shaped by:

choices.A: the personal tastes of individual performers alone.
choices.B: audiences who demand realistic performances.
choices.C: official decisions aimed at controlling public behavior.
choices.D: rivalries between theater troupes in different cities.

candidates.evidence: A government decree intended to control public behavior
candidates.explanation: The author says forces outside art, such as a decree meant to control behavior, helped create the onnagata tradition.

A.rationale: The author stresses forces outside art.

hints: What was the decree intended to do, and what did it help create?
candidates.remember: Conclusions often generalize from the passage's example.
